name: Din Tai Fung Garlic Green Beans (蒜香四季豆)
englishName: Din Tai Fung Garlic Green Beans
description: Blistered, wrinkle-skinned green beans tossed with raw garlic, salt, and white pepper. The whole dish lives or dies on the oil-blister. UNTESTED — first cook to verify.

ingredients.text: 1/4 tsp chicken bouillon powder (optional, for the restaurant umami)
ingredients.item: chicken bouillon powder (optional, for the restaurant umami)

steps.text: Trim 300 g green beans (four-season beans), trimmed and snap or cut into ~2-inch lengths. Pat BONE dry with a towel — any surface water will spit violently in hot oil. This is non-negotiable for both safety and blistering.

Add 4 tbsp neutral oil for shallow-frying to your stainless pan over medium-high. Heat until shimmering and a test bean sizzles aggressively on contact (~190°C / 375°F). On bare stainless, judge by the shimmer and a single test bean, not the IR gun — the polished surface reads low.

Lay in 300 g green beans (four-season beans), trimmed in a single layer — do NOT crowd, or they steam instead of blister. Work in two batches if needed. Leave them mostly undisturbed, tossing only occasionally, until the skins wrinkle, pucker, and pick up brown-black spots and the beans go limp-tender. 6 minutes.
Pull the beans to a paper-towel-lined plate. Pour off all but about 1 tsp of oil from the pan (save it — it's bean-flavored).

Drop heat to medium-low so the pan cools slightly. Add 5 garlic, finely minced to the residual oil and stir for 15–20 seconds — just to take the raw bite off. Garlic burns instantly here, so move fast and don't let it brown past pale gold.

Return the beans, add 1/2 tsp fine salt, 1/4 tsp white pepper, and 1/4 tsp chicken bouillon powder (optional, for the restaurant umami) if using. Toss hard for 20–30 seconds to coat every bean in garlic. Taste, adjust salt, and plate immediately.

notes:
Stainless notes: the dry-bean rule matters double here — wet beans + 190°C oil = a spatter hazard on an open pan. Keep a splatter screen handy. The fond won't build much (it's an oil-fry, not a sear), so don't chase it.

Authenticity flags: DTF's is pure — resist adding soy sauce, sugar, or sesame oil, all of which are common Western "improvements" that push it toward a generic stir-fry. The garlic goes in RAW-ish and late; it should taste sharp and fresh, not deep-roasted. If you want the cold pork-mince Sichuan version (乾煸四季豆), that's a separate recipe entirely.

Air-fryer shortcut (if you ever want it): toss beans in 1 tbsp oil + salt, 180°C for ~10 min shaking halfway, then do the garlic toss in a pan. Lower fat, ~80% of the texture.

Open question for your cook: confirm whether the blister wants to go darker (more char spots) to match what you remember from the restaurant — DTF's tend to be fairly heavily spotted.
